priorAcademicDecision.reason: A comparative-religion, culture and meaning concept was assessed first against the actual selected route. UCR has meaningful material on myth, religious visual culture, ancient religious identities, ethics and philosophical questions, but the course content cannot sustain a complete programme centred on comparative religious traditions and their study. The selected route requires World Religions, Christian history, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, study-of-religion foundations, anthropology and psychology of religion, sacred-text hermeneutics, interreligious relations and comparative religious ethics, as well as the selected Islamic-history/philosophy units. Those are substantial subjects, not language or licensing requirements. A 24-course combination would increasingly depend on general philosophy, art history, sociology or politics without a specific content-level account of their contribution to this religion-centred concept. Religion/political conflict, sustainability, Islamic studies and confessional/practical theology were also considered; none solves that coherence problem. The no-match conclusion concerns the assembled programme, not the absence of a degree title or exact one-to-one course equivalents.
priorAcademicDecision.curriculumContext: The selected comparative Religie en Levensbeschouwing route is complete at 180 EC, including 30 EC genuine profiling space. Its Dutch part-time pacing remains six calendar years; compulsory Greek/Hebrew or a confessional route are not invented. The selected Islamic-history and Islamic-philosophy choices are retained. The comparative traditions, research labs and thesis remain required.
priorAcademicDecision.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed the current 151-row enriched UCR workbook, using names, descriptions, outline-derived profiles, disciplines, topics, methods, formal prerequisites and the six Fall 2026-start availability columns. The following concrete courses were assessed rather than assuming that a missing track label decides the outcome. MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature studies ancient, Indian, Byzantine and Arabic narrative traditions and transmission across texts/images; it provides meaningful comparative myth study, not a World Religions survey or sacred-text hermeneutics sequence. MCCLITR112 Great Literary Works includes representations of organised religion, duty and memory but remains a broad Western literary survey. MCCHEAM112 Introduction to World Archaeology directly examines religious, social and gendered identities through ancient artefacts; MCCHEAM211 African Art & Heritage examines religious meaning in western-African visual traditions; MCCHEAM212 Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean includes Islamic courts and cross-cultural artistic exchange; MCCHEAM315 Heritage & Ancient Democracy studies Athenian democracy intertwined with myth and religion. These are valuable specific contributions to religious culture, not cumulative courses in the traditions or religion-study methodologies of the target. GOSPHIL111 Introduction to Western Philosophy includes god, meaning and central Western arguments; GOSPHIL214 Philosophy of Mind includes Buddhist accounts of self. GOSPHIL212 Ethics studies major moral theories and applied issues but is not comparative religious ethics. MCCHEAM212 and other rows without an enriched outline were assessed only at their documented description scope. No religious content was inferred from an attractive course title. GOSLAWJ111 Human Rights: Law & Philosophy explicitly includes Aquinas, natural law and rights in traditional societies and can inform religion/freedom questions. GOSPOLI313 Peace & Conflict covers ideological conflict, historical grievances and reconciliation; HCBPSYC315 Youth Resilience to Extremism conducts radicalisation-resilience research. Neither is relabelled as religion-specific violence or theology. GOSSOCI111/214/311 provide social theory, modernity, civil society and migrant inclusion; HCBPSYC111 examines social influences on beliefs and behaviour; GOSSOCI212 provides qualitative methods. These can support inquiry into religious communities but the documented content cannot be assumed to teach anthropology, sociology or psychology of religion. General media and communication courses can assist representation or science communication, but they do not establish a religion/media sequence. More general courses cannot be added solely to reach 24 courses or six advanced courses. Feasibility was assessed at the academic coherence gate before scheduling: no 24-course set was accepted, so no invented timetable or course credits are encoded. The comparative route does not require the biblical languages; their absence is therefore not used against its closest-match concept. Hebrew/Greek, Quranic Arabic, exegesis, jurisprudence and church formation are relevant only to the separately considered generator-supported confessional/Islamic directions. The workbook supplies no such sustained sequence, nor supervised spiritual-care or church-leadership formation.
